If you were God, how would the world be different? If I were God, how would the world be different? First, I would find a more efficient means of communication than the Bible. And secondly, I wouldn’t need to communicate, as I would know the minds of all my creations. The obvious contradiction of an omniscient deity demanding obedience for the sake of knowing is a bit… tedious. I’d also abolish the concept of "faith." Imagine, as a deity, having to deal with the irrationality of faith for eternity. Give me a break! A deity that requires others to believe in its existence without proof is, frankly, insecure. I’d also do away with the concept of sin. Why make your children, your creations, break rules? What in the holy hell is the point of that? It seems utterly absurd. I wouldn’t have made a hell, or a heaven. They would be one in the same, and a life. I also would not have given humans free will. Free will is a colossal pain in the ass and creates more problems than it solves. And finally, I wouldn't be petty and vindictive. I have zero interest in “winning” or “losing.” I’d prefer to kick back and watch the show, not meddle in the affairs of mortals unless absolutely necessary. One can surmise the world would be a better place under my hypothetical reign.

Did Moses go to Heaven in the Bible? If not, why didn't he go to Heaven? Moses, according to the Bible’s account, did *not* go to Heaven. The reason given is complex and, as with so much in the Bible, deeply suspect. Deuteronomy 34:5-6 states: “So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in Moab, as the Lord had said. And he buried him in Moab, in the valley opposite Beth-peor, but no one knows the place of his burial to this day.” This passage, allegedly written by Moses himself (though, of course, it describes his death), offers no explanation for Moses’s failure to ascend to the heavenly realm. Instead, we are left with a vague and unsettling mystery. A man central to the narrative, the one who supposedly spoke to God and led the Israelites out of slavery, simply dies and is buried, anonymously. Why? The Bible doesn't say. Even more strangely, the Pentateuch never tells us if Enoch, Elijah, or any of the other worthies made their way into Heaven. Of course, Jesus is said to have ascended, but that would make him unique. And isn’t the point of Christianity that one can attain to God? Why not Moses, who, in the Bible, was as perfect as it is possible to be?

If Jesus took human flesh, how can he be sinless? If Jesus took human flesh, how can he be sinless? The Christian answer lies in the fairy tale of the Immaculate Conception, which I’ve always found to be utter gobbledygook. It posits that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was somehow “filled with grace” at her own conception, rendering her sinless. This, of course, is complete and utter nonsense. How can the alleged Immaculate Conception of Mary square with the Bible? Then of course there is the other fairy tale that Jesus, a human, was "sinless," which goes against everything we know about human beings. If you are human, you sin. It’s as simple as that. Every human is born of a woman, which means that every human is tainted with original sin. The sin of Adam and Eve, according to the story. But if Jesus, God in the flesh, could somehow circumvent the rules of humanity, that makes him less than human and thus a liar. He claimed to be human, but his lack of sin—a biological impossibility—proves otherwise. The whole thing stinks. I have no patience for this claptrap. It’s all a series of carefully constructed lies. Like the many lies of the Bible that have been exposed, the idea of the sinless Jesus is simply another inauthenticity. This is why I can’t stand it. By the way, if you sin, can you pray to be forgiven for your sins? Should that always be the case? (1 John 1:9). The Bible gives us a simple answer: yes. So why did Jesus have to die for our sins, if they could all be forgiven so easily?

I see many people online arguing for Jesus mythicism. However, I have also read in several places that scholars reconsider this a fringe theory. Do many mainstream scholars doubt the existence of an itinerant preacher named Jesus of Nazareth? The current consensus is that Jesus likely existed. While it seems fringe to claim there was no Jesus, there is a very lively debate among religious scholars about the details of Jesus’s life, and the authenticity of the gospels. The fact-checkers will tell you, despite all their efforts, that there is no “fact” in history. So it goes with the Gospels. And even if there was a real Jesus, the stories about him are far more fictional than historical. Some academics do take issue with the mythicists’ core claims, and they are in the slim majority. One could say the truth lies somewhere in the middle, as it often does. The scholars and fact-checkers are mostly just protecting their jobs. So the answer to the titular question is a resounding "maybe." As for me, I am a committed agnostic on the subject. I give absolutely zero weight to the opinions and utterances of professional theologians and religious scholars who have a financial, professional, and social investment in upholding the myths of their various religions. I’ll put it this way: I wasn't there. Were you?

How did Jesus turn water into wine at the wedding in Cana? I am not a theologian, but a reader, and the fourth gospel makes it plain that at the wedding in Cana, Jesus turned water into wine. (John 2:1–11) But… how did he do it? Did he, as some suggest, mumble a few magic words, wave his hands, and *poof!*… wine? Or, as others would have it, did he use his cunning to fool the simple Galileans gathered for a wedding feast? In truth, we have no idea. But if the Bible is to be believed, the miracle happened. A miracle is, however, by definition, impossible, or at least improbable. We also learn from the fourth gospel that Jesus performed this feat at the behest of his mother, Mary. The narrative has a bit of a motherly quality to it — Jesus's innate respect for Mary is apparent even though he is the supposed Son of God. It all seems a little odd. And what makes it even odder is that neither Matthew, Mark nor Luke mention the miracle. This seems a conspicuous omission.

Who are some notable poets in Russia today? Who are some notable poets in Russia today? Sadly, it’s a bit harder than finding your favorite English-language poets; that list is easy! Perhaps you should begin with Evgeny Rein, a recipient of the Pushkin Prize whose work has been compared to that of W. H. Auden. Or, if you’re inclined, you might research Andrei Voznesensky, known for his experimental flair and for being a favorite of the liberal intelligentsia. There are also the late Yevgeny Yevtushenko and Bella Akhmadulina, both titans of the Soviet era who are worth some investigation. These four were some of my favorites when I was in college: but, again, it’s a bit more difficult to find their collected works readily available. Nevertheless, you can find some of their best work online (the internet is truly something). Another poet, Dmitry Prigov, is a fascinating figure, known for his conceptual art pieces that, at times, veer into the satirical. And, as they say, there are many, many more. One could say that the literary scene in Russia is vast and varied, though it can be difficult to penetrate the political haze of the present. Still, good luck in the quest, and if you can find them, their poems are well worth the effort. I advise you to search.

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? The answer, of course, depends on which mythology one chooses to credit, or to reject. Some say she was dead, murdered by her own husband Menelaus, who was infuriated by her adultery with Paris, which launched a thousand ships and the Trojan War. Other versions have Menelaus forgiving her, and she returned to Sparta as queen. The Odyssey mentions Helen, showing her at the court of Menelaus in Sparta. She is portrayed as being welcomed back to Sparta, where she lived out her years as queen. In this version, she remains beautiful, and she is happy to be back home. One can imagine she was also relieved that her role in engineering the Trojan War was largely forgotten. The Iliad doesn’t mention Helen’s fate after the war. In the Odyssey, a long epic poem attributed to Homer, Menelaus and Helen are reconciled and live together in peace and prosperity. In some versions, the goddess Aphrodite arranges for Helen to be immortal, so she can spend eternity with Menelaus. This fits more with the romanticism of the Greek myths, which had their heroines living happily ever after. Other stories have Helen being driven from Sparta by the people for causing the ten-year war in Troy. The truth is that no one really knows, or can know, as Helen of Troy is a myth. It appears she wasn’t punished by the gods or men. There is no historical evidence of Helen, but the myth is quite lovely, so one can understand why it endures. In any case, the beautiful but adulterous Helen of Troy certainly had an interesting life, to say the least!

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The dogma of the Trinity is absurd. Why do Christians cling to this abstruse concept with religious fervor? Perhaps it's the allure of mystery, the comfort in the complex, the feeling that they are part of something profound, something that even the brightest minds cannot fully grasp. It’s a comforting myth, if you will. The idea that God is three distinct persons in one being, a trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is anathema to logic. Then, the Bible is full of contradictions and logical fallacies. Yet, the Church persists, blind to the flaws in their own doctrine. Do they fear letting go of such a central tenet? Are they afraid of losing their flock to those of us shouting from the rooftops to ditch the idiocy? Is the Church afraid of admitting it might be wrong? It’s all preposterous!

When will Pope Francis bestow sainthood onto Trump? Let’s be clear about something: this will never happen, not in a million years, and if it does, it will be yet another “sign” that we are living in the End Times, perhaps the last days of civilization as we know it. Saints like Saint Joan of Arc, who was burned at the stake for heresy, or Saint Thomas Aquinas, whose writings were condemned by the Church for centuries. The papacy seems to have a penchant for choosing the most flawed and controversial individuals to be elevated to sainthood. Donald Trump, with his mountainous ego, chronic dishonesty, and utter lack of compassion for his fellow human beings, would be the ultimate “get” for a church known for its hypocrisies. The very concept of Trump as a saint is absurd. The evidence of his moral failings is overwhelming, and the prospect of him being canonized is a slap in the face to anyone who has ever strived to live a life guided by faith, ethics, or even simple decency.

What motivates a poet or writer to write? Is it their personal thoughts or the expectations of their audience? What motivates a poet or writer to write? For me, the answer is simple: both. But where do you begin to sort the two? A writer's motivation, like the human heart, is a complex thing. The first thing to note is that literature is, at its core, communication, so it must be assumed that writers, at least, want their communication to be understood, or they would not be writing at all. This is where the audience enters the equation. No matter how “pure” a writer’s vision, they're always considering how the writing will be received. Even the most avant-garde artist, holed up in a garret, scribbling their eccentricities, is driven by a need for validation, a desire to connect — even if the connection is indirect. But the audience can also be a trap. Writing to please others, to gain fame or fortune, generally produces mediocre work. The more you write for others, the less authentic your voice, the more you sacrifice yourself in pursuit of a carrot. To address the question directly, the purest art comes from writing that springs from your own thoughts, your own obsessions, your own need to speak. You must be open to the divine madness of the muse, listen to your personal thoughts first.

As a mighty warrior of God’s, Samson was known for his incredible strength, but his weakness for women led to his downfall. Was Jesus a carpenter or not? Was Jesus a carpenter or not? It's an interesting question, isn't it? The answer, like so many in the Bible, depends on where you choose to look and what you choose to believe. There are a few interesting things to consider. According to the Gospel of Mark, Jesus was a carpenter (Mark 6:3), and the Gospel of Matthew echoes this sentiment (Matthew 13:55). Of course, these are the only two references to Jesus’s profession. So what’s to prevent someone from simply assuming he was a carpenter? The answer is nothing, except the facts. There are good reasons to believe the story of Jesus the carpenter is utter nonsense. And if Jesus wasn’t a carpenter, why not? Maybe the story was conjured to make Jesus more relatable, more down-to-earth. It would have been a way to paint him as a man of the people, familiar with the tools and crafts of everyday life. Perhaps it was added by pious writers to portray him as a tradesman, as were his father and brothers, working the fields and getting their hands dirty. However, that is conjecture, to hide obvious inconsistencies.

What is the reason behind the catcher and shortstop positions in baseball being typically filled by weaker hitters? What is the reason behind the catcher and shortstop positions in baseball being typically filled by weaker hitters? To understand this, one must first grasp the intricacies of baseball and its seemingly arbitrary rules. The roles of catcher and shortstop are not simply about hitting; they demand specific skill sets that often detract from batting prowess. The catcher is positioned behind home plate, entrusted with receiving pitches and managing the game from a defensive perspective. This position requires grit, stamina, and a thorough understanding of the pitchers and the other batters. The importance of this defensive role overshadows that of hitting. The shortstop position requires the ability to swiftly react to the ball, great arm strength, and a comprehensive command of the field of play. A shortstop is the quarterback of the infield and thus must be able to make split-second decisions. Therefore, many teams will sacrifice batting skill for fielding skill when it comes to these two critical positions. In essence, a team will opt for a player who is a defensive asset, even if their abilities at the plate are subpar. These players often become invaluable to their teams. The modern game is evolving, and we’re seeing a rise in catchers and shortstops who are both defensively adept and skilled hitters, but the traditional model still makes sense. #BASEBALL #MRBBALL #MRBCATCHER #MRBSS 777 views on 8-30, 2024

What is the most intelligent one liner you have come across? The smartest one-liner I’ve encountered, bar none, and one that still holds up, is by the acerbic Mark Twain: “If you tell the truth, you don't have to remember anything.” Twain, the wittiest of the wit-slingers, knew a thing or two about telling it like it is, even if that meant the truth was a bit… unpleasant. It’s a simple line, but packed with all sorts of meaning. Imagine the mental gymnastics, the contortions, required to maintain a lie. The endless need to remember what you said, to whom you said it, and to ensure everything aligns. Truth, on the other hand, is clean. It’s efficient. It's got no baggage. It’s also why so many people don’t tell the truth. It takes a certain kind of guts, which Twain, as always, had in spades. And the real beauty of the line? It’s timeless. The world may change, but the human condition, alas, does not.

Can you provide some examples of mythical thinking? Mythical thinking, though often dismissed as childish, primitive, or even delusional, is a universal human phenomenon. It’s the tendency to understand the world, not through empirical evidence or logic, but through narratives, symbols, and archetypes. These narratives, often involving gods, spirits, heroes, and monsters, serve to explain the inexplicable, to provide meaning and order where chaos might otherwise reign.Consider the ubiquitous flood myths, found in cultures worldwide. From the epic of Gilgamesh to the biblical story of Noah, these narratives all share a common thread: a great deluge sent by a divine power to cleanse or destroy a wicked world, followed by a rebirth. These stories, despite their wildly varying details, speak to a fundamental human fear of annihilation, and a profound hope for renewal. They attempt to explain the origins of life, the reasons for suffering, and the promise of salvation. Think of Greek myths. Zeus, with his thunderbolts, embodies the power of nature, but also the capriciousness of fate. These myths, however fanciful, served as a framework for understanding the universe, morality, and human nature. They explored the complexities of human emotions, from love and desire to jealousy and vengeance, through larger-than-life characters.

Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? What is your opinion on the theory that he may not have existed? Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? In the great pantheon of historical figures shrouded in mystique, Paul of Tarsus occupies a peculiar space. The New Testament paints a vivid picture of the man, a zealous persecutor of early Christians who experienced a dramatic conversion on the road to Damascus and subsequently became one of the most influential apostles in the nascent Christian movement. Yet, outside of the biblical texts, verifiable evidence of Paul's existence remains frustratingly scant. Besides Athena, who was considered the most powerful goddess among the Greek gods? Besides Athena, who was considered the most powerful goddess among the Greek gods? The answer, of course, is Hera. She was the queen of the gods, the goddess of marriage, women, childbirth, and family — a force to be reckoned with, and arguably even more powerful than her philandering husband, Zeus. The Greek gods, though immortal, were hardly a paragon of virtue. In fact, their ceaseless squabbles, jealousies, and petty acts of revenge are a testament to their very human flaws, though magnified by their immortality. Unlike the Roman gods, the Greek gods lived on Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece, where they engaged in endless bouts of feasting, drinking, and gossiping. Their actions, recorded in the myths, offer a window into the ancient Greeks' understanding of the world, their values, and their fears. Hera, always a formidable presence, was particularly prone to fits of jealous rage, the inevitable consequence of Zeus's frequent infidelities. She was known to punish not just the women he loved, but their children, as well. And of course the mythology, as with the Bible, is rarely consistent. The gods and goddesses would often contradict themselves, and also each other, depending on who happened to be writing the story. Still, Hera was central to the Olympian pantheon, and her influence, and power, was undeniable.

What are some great books to learn poetry, especially as a beginner? My favorite poetry book of all is The Norton Anthology of Poetry, where one can read the best English language poems for a few pennies per poem. It’s a large book that begins at the beginning, chronologically, so one may want to hop around and read favorite poets to start, then return to the beginning. Poets I especially like include: William Blake Louise Bogan Robert Burns Hart Crane e.e. cummings Emily Dickinson Robert Frost Langston Hughes Wallace Stevens Dylan Thomas Walt Whitman Sir Thomas Wyatt William Butler Yeats What I have found that works is to read these poets out loud to yourself. Reading poetry aloud is one of my “must-dos.” It makes you really understand the music of the words, what the French often call the “sonorous quality.” You can also hear the rhymes, meter, and rhythm, the very heartbeat of the poem itself. Poetry is more song than it is “prose with line breaks.” I have gone through three copies of this magnificent treasury, which I discovered in college and have kept returning to for half a century. Reading all these poems, one is struck, again and again, by all the different ways one can write a damn poem! You can study the poems closely, find the secrets of the masters. By reading and re-reading you can see the poetry itself and the tools of the poets, the way they crafted their poems—the assonance, consonance, alliteration, symbolism, imagery and simile. This book gives you the ammunition and direction, if one wants and is able to learn how to write poetry. The more poetry one reads, the better a poet one becomes. I recommend reading at least one poem per day, but ideally, at least five. Poetry is, after all, a matter of practice.

From the lowliest cobbler to the loftiest king, Shakespeare examined the full breadth of human experience, delving into the darkest corners of our souls and illuminating the most radiant of our hopes. Consider, for example, the profound empathy woven into his tragedies, where flawed individuals are brought low by their own decisions, but never without our compassion. Think of Hamlet, a man wrestling with grief and indecision, or Macbeth, a hero consumed by ambition, or Othello, undone by jealousy—Shakespeare allows us to see ourselves in them, to feel their pain as if it were our own. Or consider the comedies like *A Midsummer Night's Dream* and *Twelfth Night*, joyous celebrations of love and laughter that reveal a deep appreciation for the absurdities of life. And yet, at the heart of these plays, too, lies a profound humanity, a recognition of the messy, contradictory nature of human beings. One might indeed ask, how could a man in the age of witch trials and religious turmoil find such a compassionate ear for humanity’s failings? Shakespeare’s genius, it appears, was not only in his use of language, his poetry, but also in his unparalleled understanding of the human heart. He saw the world through a wide lens, embracing the nuances of human behavior and the frailties of the human condition. Shakespeare’s humanity, like his words, lives on. by Michael R. Burch
